think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A pediatric patient from rural northwest India presenting with chronic progressive signs of raised intracranial pressure and focal hemiparesis associated with a large cerebral cystic lesion mimics primary neuroepithelial tumors or neurocysticercosis, with the absence of pulmonary or hepatic cysts creating diagnostic uncertainty.
2. Admission Breakpoint: Admission triage concludes following clinical neurologic evaluation, baseline visceral screening (chest radiograph and abdominal ultrasound), and neuroimaging (CT/MRI) defining the intracranial cystic mass, before neurosurgical exploration.
3. Differential Distinctions: Intracranial neoplasms (cystic astrocytomas) and neurocysticercosis present with nodular ring enhancement and prominent vasogenic edema; primary cerebral hydatid cysts present as spherical non-enhancing unilocular fluid collections, confirmed by intact surgical cyst excision.
case_prompt: A 12-year-old child from a rural area of southeast Rajasthan presented with a progressive history of headache, occasional vomiting, decreased visual acuity, and right-sided hemiparesis. The family reported domestic contact with pet dogs. On admission physical examination, the patient had right hemiparesis and bilateral papilledema on fundoscopic evaluation. Plain radiography of the chest and ultrasonography of the abdomen revealed no focal lesions, cysts, or masses in the pulmonary fields or abdominal viscera. Cranial computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a solitary, sharply demarcated, spherical cystic lesion in the temporoparietal region with mass effect.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Intracranial Cystic Neoplasm (e.g., Low-Grade Cystic Astrocytoma)
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered the primary suspect given the focal neurological deficit, hemiparesis, papilledema, and intracranial space-occupying lesion in a child; parasitic cysts constitute only a tiny fraction of operated cerebral mass lesions.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: representing an incidence of 1% of all space-occupying lesions operated during this period.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Disseminated Visceral Hydatidosis with Brain Metastasis
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Cerebral hydatid involvement usually occurs secondary to primary filter organ infestation in the liver or lungs; excluded by normal systemic screening examinations.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: These investigations failed to reveal any associated hydatid cyst in the lungs and abdomen.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Definitive diagnosis of intracranial hydatid disease was established upon complete neurosurgical extirpation of the intact parasitic cyst using rupture-preventing techniques, followed by prolonged adjuvant albendazole therapy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The hydatid cysts were totally excised in all the three cases and necessary precautions to prevent rupture and dissemination of hydatid were taken during the surgery; despite these precautions, rupture of cysts occurred in one case (33.3%).

editor_comments: Admission narrative strictly stops before neurosurgical resection. Visceral imaging reported neutrally without spoiler terminology.
